s: Surgical time-out: confirm patient, side and procedure
Everyone stops and checks out loud: right patient, right side, right operation. Prevents wrong-site surgery.
General anaesthesia, head fixed in a pinned head holder
Three pins hold the skull perfectly still so the neuronavigation stays accurate.
Register neuronavigation to the MRI
Like GPS: the computer matches the patient's head to their scan so the surgeon can see where the tumour is under the skin.
Skin incision and fold back the scalp flap
Incision planned behind the hairline where possible; the scalp is reflected to expose bone.
Drill burr holes and cut a bone flap
A high-speed drill makes small holes, then a craniotome connects them and the bone flap is lifted out (kept to put back).
Open the dura
The tough outer membrane is opened in a flap, exposing the brain.
Remove the tumour under the microscope
Microsurgical removal, often with ultrasonic aspiration, staying away from critical areas (sometimes with the patient awake for speech mapping).
Close the dura watertight
Prevents CSF leak and infection.
Replace the bone flap with small plates and close the scalp
The bone is fixed back with titanium plates and screws; the scalp is closed in layers.
Time-out, general anaesthesia, head turned, prep from head to belly
The whole path of the shunt (scalp, neck, chest, abdomen) is prepped as one sterile field.
Small scalp incision and a burr hole
Usually behind the ear or at Kocher's point near the front.
Small abdominal incision to reach the peritoneum
The peritoneal cavity will absorb the CSF.
Tunnel the distal catheter under the skin from scalp to abdomen
A long tunnelling rod passes under the skin of the neck and chest.
Pass the ventricular catheter into the lateral ventricle
Aimed using landmarks or navigation; CSF flowing out confirms the position.
Connect catheter, valve and distal tubing
The valve sets the pressure at which CSF drains so it doesn't over-drain.
Check flow, place the distal end in the peritoneum
CSF should drip from the end before it's placed in the belly.
Close both incisions
Infection is the main early complication, so closure is careful.
Check for raised pressure and bleeding risk (scan if needed)
With a brain mass or raised pressure, removing CSF could cause herniation, so a CT comes first when there are warning signs.
Consent and position: curled on the side or sitting forward
Flexing the spine opens the gaps between the vertebrae.
Find the L3–L4 or L4–L5 space (line between the iliac crests)
The spinal cord ends around L1–L2 in adults, so this level is below it.
Clean the skin, sterile drape, numb with local anaesthetic
Aseptic technique prevents meningitis.
Insert the spinal needle with stylet, bevel facing up the spine
Passes through ligaments into the subarachnoid space; a 'give' is often felt.
Remove stylet, see CSF, measure opening pressure
A manometer measures the pressure before any fluid is collected.
Collect CSF into numbered tubes
Tubes go for cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain and culture.
Replace stylet, remove needle, cover the site
Putting the stylet back before withdrawing may reduce headache risk.
Time-out and general anaesthesia, antibiotics given
A dose of antibiotics before the cut lowers wound infection.
Port at the belly button, inflate the abdomen with CO₂
The gas lifts the abdominal wall so there's room to see and work.
Camera in, place two more working ports
Under direct vision so nothing gets injured.
Find the appendix by following the bands on the colon
The three taeniae coli of the large bowel meet at the base of the appendix.
Divide the mesoappendix and its artery
Seals off the blood supply before removal.
Staple or tie off the base, cut the appendix free
The base is secured so bowel contents can't leak.
Remove the appendix in a bag through a port
The bag stops infected tissue touching the wound.
Check for bleeding, release gas, close the ports
Small incisions mean faster recovery than open surgery.

procs.t: Burr holes for a chronic subdural haematoma
s: CT confirms the collection, clotting checked and corrected
Blood thinners are reversed before surgery when possible.
Time-out, anaesthesia (sometimes sedation + local)
Many patients are elderly, so the lightest safe anaesthetic is chosen.
Mark and make one or two small scalp incisions over the collection
Placed using the CT.
Drill burr holes through the skull
A perforator drill stops automatically once it's through the bone.
Open the dura and let the old blood drain
Dark 'motor oil' fluid comes out under pressure.
Wash out the space with warm saline
Irrigation clears the liquefied blood until the fluid runs clear.
Leave a soft drain, close the scalp
A drain for a day or two lowers the chance it comes back.
Time-out, anaesthesia, navigation registered
Navigation helps avoid the carotid arteries beside the pituitary.
Endoscope passed through the nostril
No skin cuts: the route is through the nose.
Open into the sphenoid sinus
The air sinus sits right below the pituitary.
Open the bony floor of the sella turcica
The 'Turkish saddle' of bone holds the pituitary.
Open the dura and remove the tumour, protecting the normal gland
Soft tumours are removed with curettes and suction.
Repair the floor (e.g. a flap from the nasal lining)
Seals against CSF leak.
After surgery: check sodium, urine output and hormones
Diabetes insipidus (too much urine) and hormone deficiency are watched for.
Time-out, anaesthesia, prone position on a frame
Lying face down with the belly free lowers bleeding.
X-ray to confirm the level
Counting the vertebrae on X-ray prevents wrong-level surgery.
Small midline incision, muscle moved off the lamina
Muscle is pushed aside, not cut through.
Remove a little bone and ligament (laminotomy)
Opens a window into the spinal canal.
Gently retract the nerve root
Under the microscope, the compressed nerve is moved aside.
Remove the herniated disc fragment
The piece pressing on the nerve is taken out; this relieves leg pain (sciatica).
Check the nerve is free, close in layers
Most patients walk the same day.
Consent, time-out, full sterile gown, gloves, drape
Central line infections are dangerous, so full barrier precautions are used.
Ultrasound to find the internal jugular vein
Ultrasound guidance lowers artery puncture and lung injury.
Numb the skin with local anaesthetic
Needle into the vein, dark non-pulsatile blood drawn back
Confirms venous (not arterial) access.
Pass the guidewire through the needle, remove the needle
The wire holds the path. Never let go of the wire.
Small skin nick and a dilator over the wire
Widens the tract for the catheter.
Thread the catheter over the wire, remove the wire
Count the wire out: a lost guidewire is a serious error.
Flush, secure, dressing, chest X-ray to check the tip
The X-ray confirms the tip position and rules out a collapsed lung.
Prepare: suction, oxygen, tube, laryngoscope, plan B
'Prepare for failure': backup airway devices ready.
Position: 'sniffing the morning air'
Neck flexed, head extended lines up the mouth, throat and larynx.
Pre-oxygenate with 100% oxygen for a few minutes
Fills the lungs with oxygen so there's time before levels drop.
Give sedation and a paralytic (rapid sequence)
Drug names only here, e.g. an induction agent then a neuromuscular blocker.
Laryngoscope in, see the vocal cords
The blade lifts the tongue and epiglottis.
Pass the tube through the cords, inflate the cuff
The cuff seals the airway.
Confirm: CO₂ detector colour change, chest rise, breath sounds
End-tidal CO₂ is the gold standard check.
Secure the tube and start the ventilator
Then a chest X-ray checks the depth.
Check the wound: nerves, tendons, blood flow, tetanus status
Test movement and feeling beyond the cut before numbing.
Numb with local anaesthetic
Injected into the wound edges.
Irrigate thoroughly with saline
Washing out is the most important step to prevent infection.
Explore for debris, sterile drape
Look for glass or dirt.
Place interrupted sutures, edges slightly turned out
Everted edges heal flatter.
Dressing and wound-care advice
Keep clean; when to come back.
Remove sutures later (face ~5 days, limbs longer)
Face heals fastest because of its blood supply.

procs.t: Getting sterile for the operating room
s: Hat, mask, eye protection on
Put on before scrubbing, since you can't touch them after.
Remove jewellery, clean under the nails
Germs hide under rings and nails.
Surgical scrub: hands then forearms to above the elbows
Hands always held higher than elbows so water runs away from the hands.
Dry with a sterile towel
Hands first, then down each arm.
Gown on with help from the circulating nurse
The front from chest to waist and the sleeves are the sterile zone.
Closed gloving
Hands stay inside the sleeves while the gloves go on.
Keep hands above the waist, in front of you
Below the waist or behind the back counts as non-sterile.
MRI planning: pick the target (e.g. subthalamic nucleus)
The path is planned to avoid blood vessels and ventricles.
Stereotactic frame or frameless system fitted, time-out
Gives sub-millimetre accuracy.
Burr hole at the planned entry point
Usually one on each side.
Microelectrode recording while advancing
Each nucleus has a typical firing pattern, so the team can 'hear' when they're in the target.
Test stimulation with the patient awake
They check tremor and stiffness improve without side effects.
Implant the permanent electrode and fix it
The lead stays in place for years.
Tunnel the wire to a battery under the collarbone
The pulse generator is like a pacemaker for the brain.
